text:
Corn's potassium (K) requirement is roughly as large as its nitrogen requirement (see the nutrient uptake reference table), though K deficiency is less commonly seen in Cambodia than N or P deficiency -- it occurs mainly on sandy, low-reserve soils. K deficiency shows up as yellowing or browning along the margins and tips of leaves, especially older leaves (marginal leaf scorch).

Where a soil test or visible symptoms confirm K deficiency, muriate of potash (KCl, about 50% K2O) can be applied at 60-100 kg/ha. This is best applied at or shortly before planting, and the source advises against delaying application beyond roughly 4 weeks after crop emergence.

Because phosphorus and potassium can both become fixed/immobile in soil (less available over time after application), understanding basic soil fertility principles helps farmers get better value from P and K fertilizer -- band placement near the root zone, rather than broadcasting on the surface, generally gives better uptake efficiency for both nutrients.
